sentences.text: Distribution monitoring begins at the High Service Pump Header, where discharge pressure, total flow, and pump status provide the control room with the first indication of system demand changes.

The Distribution Dispatcher watches each pressure zone for sustained deviations rather than reacting to every short pressure fluctuation caused by hydrant use, valve movement, or customer demand changes.
Normal control-room practice is to compare pressure trends with reservoir level trends, pump starts, and recent field activity before changing a setpoint.
The North Distribution Pressure Station is monitored as a separate zone asset with its own suction pressure, discharge pressure, pump availability, and communication status.
The South Distribution Pressure Station starts its lead booster pump when discharge pressure remains below the configured start band for the required delay period.

When a distribution station is in automatic operation, local controls are expected to sequence pumps within approved limits and report abnormal starts, failures, or valve positions to the control system.
When a distribution station is in local or manual operation, the Distribution Dispatcher records the reason, the expected duration, and the field contact responsible for the change.
The Clearwell Level Controller is checked before large distribution adjustments so that high service pumping does not create avoidable level instability.
The Chief Operator may direct a conservative pumping posture during unusual demand, main repair activity, or recovery from a treatment upset.
The Duty Engineer reviews persistent low-pressure complaints, repeated station alarms, or mismatches between observed pressure and modeled expectations.
Cobalt shall provide a reliable filter service status indication before the control room treats increased distribution demand as available finished-water capacity.
Sparrow records incoming distribution check samples with the pressure zone, collection point, and time needed for control-room review.
The SCADA Historian Server uses the Sample Chain Slip to associate distribution water-quality entries with the operating period shown in the electronic log.
The Distribution Dispatcher sends the Pressure Zone Handoff Card after verifying current pressure-zone setpoints, active alarms, and open field work.
Shift handoff includes any disabled alarms, temporary operating limits, pending station inspections, and customer complaint trends that may affect dispatch decisions.
If communication to a distribution station is lost, the control room assumes the last confirmed operating mode remains in effect until field verification or telemetry restoration proves otherwise.
Field crews notify the control room before opening or closing major distribution valves so that pressure changes can be distinguished from pump or instrumentation problems.
The Distribution Dispatcher coordinates planned hydrant flushing, valve exercising, and main isolation work with pumping schedules to limit avoidable pressure swings.
When a Chlorine Residual Alarm is active, distribution pressure decisions remain coordinated with water-quality response actions rather than being treated as a purely hydraulic issue.

The Laboratory Sample Receiving Bench provides analytical status through normal plant reporting channels, and the control room uses that status to interpret pressure-zone complaints involving taste, odor, or disinfectant concerns.
The SCADA Historian Server retains pressure, flow, pump status, and alarm data needed to reconstruct dispatch decisions after an event.
During Storm Intake Mode, the Distribution Dispatcher avoids unnecessary zone changes unless demand, storage, or public-safety conditions require action.
Control-room coordination with field crews is conducted by radio or phone using clear station names, valve identifiers, expected direction of pressure change, and confirmation when work is complete.

Normal distribution operation is restored when pressure zones are stable, station alarms are cleared or assigned, field work is accounted for, and the Chief Operator has no remaining operating restrictions.
